routes.label: Subtract the probability of two odd numbers

question:
Spinners \(A\) and \(B\) are spun. On each spinner, the arrow is equally likely to land on each number. What is the probability that the product of the two spinners’ numbers is even?

[Figure 1](figures/2004_AMC_8_Q21_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Assume the spins are independent, as in the usual spinner model. Spinner \(A\) has the numbers \(1,2,3,4\), and spinner \(B\) has \(1,2,3\). Each of the four results on \(A\) can be paired with each of the three results on \(B\), giving \(4\cdot3=12\) equally likely ordered outcomes.

A product is odd exactly when both factors are odd. Writing the result from \(A\) first, the odd-product outcomes are
\[
(1,1),\quad(1,3),\quad(3,1),\quad(3,3).
\]
These are all the possibilities because each spinner has only the odd numbers \(1\) and \(3\). Every other outcome has an even factor and therefore an even product. The required probability is
\[
\frac{12-4}{12}=\frac{8}{12}=\boxed{\frac23},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Use the usual assumption that the two spins are independent. Since \(A\) has four possible results and \(B\) has three, there are \(4\cdot3=12\) equally likely ordered outcomes.

Separate the outcomes according to whether \(A\)'s number is even or odd. If \(A\) lands on \(2\) or \(4\), any of \(B\)'s three numbers gives an even product. This accounts for \(2\cdot3=6\) outcomes. If \(A\) lands on \(1\) or \(3\), the product is even only when \(B\) lands on \(2\), giving two more outcomes.

Every result of \(A\) belongs to exactly one of these cases, so no outcome is omitted or counted twice. Hence the probability is
\[
\frac{6+2}{12}=\boxed{\frac23},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count the even products directly
